followUps:
A captive dependency is a long-lived service that holds a short-lived one, so the short-lived one never gets released. If a singleton takes a scoped DbContext in its constructor, that one context lives for the whole application.

It then is shared by every request and thread, which is unsafe because the context is not thread-safe. Its change tracker also keeps growing and serves stale data. ASP.NET Core catches this with scope validation in Development. Fix it by injecting IDbContextFactory<T> or an IServiceScopeFactory and creating a scope per unit of work.

It resets the instance's state so the next request sees a clean context. When a pooled context is returned, EF clears the change tracker, detaches all entities, and resets things like query tracking behavior, saved-changes counters and event state, then puts the instance back in the pool.

Anything you add yourself, such as a field holding the current tenant id, is not reset unless you handle it, so a pooled context must not keep per-request state. The gain is avoiding the cost of building a new context object each request, which only matters at high throughput.

code.title: Entity states: what SaveChanges does for each

followUps:
Nothing is sent to the database, because the entity never existed there. Calling Remove on an entity in the Added state simply detaches it, since there is no row to delete.

For example, db.Add(blog); db.Remove(blog); db.SaveChanges(); runs no INSERT and no DELETE. If the entity was Unchanged or Modified, Remove would instead mark it Deleted and issue a DELETE. The special case exists only for Added entities with store-generated keys; this keeps unsaved objects from creating needless commands.

It runs automatically at the start of SaveChanges, and also when you call ChangeTracker.Entries(), Entry() on a tracked entity, or Local, and before queries that need tracked state. It compares each tracked entity's current values with its snapshot.

With thousands of tracked entities this scan is slow, as the cost is proportional to the number of entities times their properties. You can turn it off with ChangeTracker.AutoDetectChangesEnabled = false for bulk inserts, but then you must call DetectChanges() yourself or changes are missed. Change-tracking proxies avoid the scan.

code.title: No-tracking vs identity resolution

followUps:
Because without tracking, EF has no identity map, so every row that mentions the same entity creates a new object. A JOIN that returns the same customer for 1,000 orders gives you 1,000 separate customer objects instead of one.

The demo shows two orders with the same customer producing two different objects. The fix is AsNoTrackingWithIdentityResolution, which uses a temporary map during the query, so memory goes back to one object per distinct row. A projection into a DTO avoids the issue too.

Yes, you can attach it, but you should do it deliberately. db.Attach(entity) starts tracking it as Unchanged, then you change properties or set Entry(entity).State = Modified and call SaveChanges. Update(entity) marks every property as modified, which makes an UPDATE of all columns.

The catch is that if the context is already tracking another instance with the same key, EF throws an identity conflict. Also, with a no-tracking graph, attached related entities may be treated as Added or Modified. For simple edits, re-query with tracking by key, which costs one query but is predictable.

code.title: N+1 queries versus a batched IN query

followUps:
For each included reference or collection, EF adds a JOIN to the single SQL statement, and the result rows are stitched back into object graphs. A reference like Include(o => o.Customer) becomes an INNER or LEFT JOIN to Customers.

SELECT o.*, c.*
FROM Orders o
LEFT JOIN Customers c ON c.Id = o.CustomerId

With a collection include, the parent is joined to children, so a parent with 3 children appears on 3 rows. EF then groups the rows by the parent key to rebuild one parent with its list. Orders must be consistent for this stitching, which is why EF adds ORDER BY on keys.

It becomes a problem when it pulls far more data than you use, or when several collections are included in one query. Each extra collection multiplies the rows, so 100 posts with 50 tags each joined to 20 comments is 100 x 50 x 20 = 100,000 rows.

It also loads entire entities when you only need a few columns, and it tracks them all, which costs memory. Alternatives: a Select projection to a DTO, AsSplitQuery() for several collections, or filtered includes such as Include(b => b.Posts.Where(p => p.Active)) to cut rows.

You need the proxies package and you must turn it on. Install Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore.Proxies, call UseLazyLoadingProxies() on the options, and make every navigation property virtual on non-sealed entity classes.

options.UseLazyLoadingProxies()
       .UseSqlServer(connectionString);

Without proxies there is another route: inject ILazyLoader into the entity constructor and call its Load in the navigation getter. Proxies create runtime subclasses, so entities must be public, unsealed, and not have constructors that can't be called.

Badly, if you are not careful: a serializer reads every public property, so it touches each navigation and triggers a database query for it. Walking a graph can load much of your database into memory.

It can also create infinite loops, because Order points to Customer and Customer points back to its Orders. This causes a cycle error or a huge response. If the context has been disposed by the time the serializer runs, the lazy load throws. The standard fix is to return DTOs from Select instead of entities, so only the data you meant to send is read.

code.title: Expression trees versus delegates

followUps:
Use the one generated SQL text that EF would run, either by logging or by asking the query for it. In EF Core 5 and later, call query.ToQueryString() before executing it to get the SQL with parameter values shown as declarations.

Other ways: optionsBuilder.LogTo(Console.WriteLine) or the logging category Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore.Database.Command, plus EnableSensitiveDataLogging() in development to see parameter values. For production, use OpenTelemetry or an APM trace. Check the SQL whenever a query touches big tables.

Keep the query as IQueryable and compose the filters conditionally, so each step adds to the expression tree. Execution happens once, at the end, in SQL.

IQueryable<Order> q = db.Orders;
if (minTotal != null) q = q.Where(o => o.Total >= minTotal);
if (status != null)   q = q.Where(o => o.Status == status);
var list = await q.ToListAsync();

For fully dynamic fields, build an Expression<Func<T,bool>> with Expression.Property and Expression.Equal, or use a library built on expression trees. Never accept a field name from users without a whitelist.

You get the conflict by merging the two snapshots by hand, as two branches modified the model at once. The snapshot file is generated, so the safest way is to regenerate it rather than edit it by hand.

Steps: merge the model classes first, then remove your own migration (dotnet ef migrations remove after taking the other branch's snapshot), and create it again so it diffs against the other branch's snapshot. Then review the new migration. If both branches already applied different migrations to a shared database, keep both and add a third that reconciles them.

The safest way is to roll forward with a new migration that undoes the change, because production data has often changed since the bad migration ran. Rolling back by running Down may destroy data created after the change, e.g. dropping a column that was just filled.

If you must go back, take a backup first, then run dotnet ef database update PreviousMigration or run the generated script for the Down steps. Write migrations with expand/contract so the old code keeps working, then a bad release can be reverted by redeploying the old code without touching the schema.

code.title: Optimistic concurrency with a version column

followUps:
Because holding database locks while a person looks at a form is costly, and web requests are stateless. A pessimistic lock would stay held across requests, so one slow or abandoned user blocks everybody else.

Optimistic concurrency holds no lock; it only checks at write time with WHERE Id = @id AND Version = @v. Conflicts are rare in most apps, so the cheap check costs little, and the rare conflict is handled by retry or a message. Pessimistic locking fits only short, hot-spot work such as taking a seat in a queue, done inside one transaction.

PostgreSQL has no rowversion type, so use the system column xmin as the token or keep your own version column. With Npgsql, map xmin as a concurrency token.

modelBuilder.Entity<Product>()
  .Property(p => p.Version)
  .IsRowVersion();   // Npgsql maps this to xmin

The mechanism stays the same: the UPDATE's WHERE includes the original value, 0 rows affected throws DbUpdateConcurrencyException. Alternatively, add an int Version with [ConcurrencyCheck] and increment it yourself on each change.

Make both use the same connection and the same transaction object. EF Core gives you the transaction with db.Database.BeginTransactionAsync(), and then you hand its underlying connection and transaction to Dapper.

await using var tx = await db.Database.BeginTransactionAsync();
var conn = db.Database.GetDbConnection();
await conn.ExecuteAsync(sql, args, tx.GetDbTransaction());
await db.SaveChangesAsync();
await tx.CommitAsync();

Dapper commands fail if they run on that connection without being given the transaction. Commit once at the end; rolling back, or disposing without commit, undoes both.

If you started the transaction yourself, EF does not roll it back automatically when SaveChanges fails; the failure leaves your transaction open and you decide. When the transaction already exists, EF uses a savepoint around its own SaveChanges so a failed save can be undone without ending your transaction.

That means the data from your earlier steps is still there, and you can retry or call RollbackAsync. If you do nothing and just dispose the transaction, it rolls back everything. Savepoints are used on providers that support them, such as SQL Server and PostgreSQL.

The rules are that the query must be a SELECT and must return every column the entity needs, with names matching the mapped column names. EF then wraps it as a subquery, so LINQ operators on top are added around it.

It can't end with a semicolon, and on SQL Server it can't use ORDER BY unless there is TOP, because a subquery cannot be ordered. Put sorting in LINQ with OrderBy instead. Stored procedures and some CTE forms can't be composed; call AsEnumerable() or AsAsyncEnumerable() after them if you need further operators.

Call it with FromSql using an EXEC statement and parameters, and make sure the result has all the columns of the entity. The result cannot be composed with further LINQ, such as Where, so apply filters inside the procedure.

var list = await db.Blogs
  .FromSql($"EXEC dbo.GetBlogs {minRating}")
  .ToListAsync();

The interpolated hole becomes a parameter, so it is safe. Use AsNoTracking() if you do not plan to edit the results. If the procedure returns a different shape, use Database.SqlQuery<T> with a DTO.

code.title: Row counts: single query vs split query

followUps:
A single join returns 100 x 50 = 5,000 rows, because every post is paired with every tag for that blog. The demo prints this count next to the split-query total.

Each of those 5,000 rows also repeats the blog's columns. A split query sends separate statements: 1 blog row, 100 post rows and 50 tag rows, so 151 rows over 3 round trips. The single-query growth is a product, the split-query growth is a sum, which is why it matters more as collections grow.

Often yes, if you only need part of the data. A Select projection into a DTO fetches just the columns you display, and a projection with sub-collections can also use filtering and counting in SQL, for instance p.Tags.Count() instead of loading all tags.

It also skips change tracking, so it saves memory and CPU. Use Include (with split queries) when you must modify the loaded entities and save them. For read-only screens and API responses, a projection is normally the best choice and avoids cartesian explosion entirely.

Constants make each distinct value a different SQL text, so the database cannot reuse a cached plan, and EF has to translate again. Parameters keep the SQL text the same.

When you write Where(x => x.Id == 5) inline, EF usually parameterizes captured variables but a literal constant may be embedded in the SQL. A thousand different literal values then give a thousand cached plans, filling the plan cache and costing compile time. A closure variable such as var id = 5; becomes @__id_0 and shares one plan. Use EF.Constant only when you want a constant on purpose, such as for skewed data.

Drop down when the generated SQL cannot be made fast enough by tuning LINQ, or when the work is set-based and unrelated to entities. Examples: complex reporting with window functions or CTEs, bulk loads, and very hot read paths where object materialization dominates.

Measure first: if 20 ms of a 25 ms query is the database, Dapper will not help. Dapper skips change tracking and expression translation, so it is faster for simple reads, but you write and maintain SQL yourself. You can mix both on the same connection, keeping EF for writes and Dapper for heavy reads, with tests on the SQL.

code.title: Dependency ordering of inserts and deletes

followUps:
You break the cycle by making one side optional, so one row can be inserted first with a null foreign key and then updated. EF can't order two required relationships that point at each other, because each INSERT needs the other row to exist.

Example: Employee has a required Department and Department has a required Manager. Make Department.ManagerId nullable, insert the department, insert the manager, then set the foreign key in a second SaveChanges call. Another option is a deferred constraint where the database supports it.

The ordering still follows the foreign keys, but there is no need to wait for the database to generate keys. With client-generated keys such as GUIDs, EF knows every key before saving, so it can fill the foreign keys at once and the keys are not temporary values.

Sequential GUIDs help because they sort roughly by creation time, which keeps clustered index inserts from scattering pages. There are fewer round trips on providers that must return a key after each insert, and you can build an entire graph without trips to the database. The topological order of INSERTs is unchanged.
